title: Module 1 assessment
subtitle: Excel Foundations
description: Fifteen questions across the whole of Module 1. Every question explains its answer, right or wrong.

questions.question: You click a cell and the Name Box shows `D12`, while the Formula Bar shows `=B12*C12`. What is actually stored in D12?
options: The number you can see in the cell
A link to B12 and C12
questions.explanation: The cell stores the formula; the grid shows its result. This is the single most useful habit in Excel - when a number looks wrong, click it and read the Formula Bar, because the grid never tells you where a number came from.

questions.question: In the address `B3`, the letter is the column and the number is the row.
questions.explanation: Column first, then row - always. B3 is column B, row 3. Getting this backwards is why people write =A1 when they meant =1A, and it matters more later when you read a range like B3:F20 at a glance.

questions.question: You have built a file containing a recorded macro. Which format must you save it as for the macro to survive?
questions.explanation: .xlsm is the macro-enabled workbook. Saving a macro file as .xlsx silently strips the code - Excel warns you, but the warning is easy to click past, and the macro is simply gone next time you open it.

questions.question: Saving a three-sheet workbook as .csv keeps all three sheets.
questions.explanation: A .csv file holds one sheet of plain text - no formulas, no formatting, no second sheet. Excel saves only the active sheet and discards the rest. For sharing data with another system .csv is right; for keeping your work it is a trap.

questions.question: Someone asks you to check the cell at column D, row 12. Write that cell address as Excel would show it in the Name Box.
questions.explanation: Column letter then row number, no space. The Name Box also works in reverse: type D12 into it and press Enter to jump straight there, which is faster than scrolling on a large sheet.

questions.question: You press Ctrl+End on a sheet that visibly ends at row 40, and Excel jumps to row 9,312. What does that tell you?
options: There is data below row 40 you cannot see
Ctrl+End always goes to the last row of the sheet
Excel still thinks cells down to row 9,312 were used at some point
questions.explanation: Ctrl+End goes to the last cell of the USED range, which remembers cells that once held data or formatting even after you cleared them. It is the usual reason a small sheet becomes a huge file - delete those rows entirely and save to reset it.

questions.question: What is the difference between Ctrl+Down Arrow and Ctrl+Shift+Down Arrow?
options: Ctrl+Shift also selects everything it travels over
Ctrl+Shift moves to the very last row
questions.explanation: Adding Shift to any navigation shortcut turns the move into a selection. That one rule gives you a dozen shortcuts for free, and it is how you select a 4,000-row column without touching the mouse.

questions.question: You select a column of 300 numbers to sanity-check them. Without typing a formula, where can you read their sum and average immediately?
options: The Status Bar at the bottom of the window
questions.explanation: The Status Bar shows Count, Sum and Average of whatever is selected, and you can right-click it to add Minimum and Maximum. It is the fastest check in Excel and most people never notice it.

questions.question: A modern Excel worksheet holds just over 65,000 rows.
questions.explanation: It holds 1,048,576 rows and 16,384 columns. Worth knowing because it tells you when you have outgrown Excel - a dataset approaching that limit belongs in a database, and the file will be painful long before you reach it.

questions.question: Your team tracks 400,000 transaction records that six people need to update at the same time. Excel or a database?
options: Excel - 400,000 rows fits inside the row limit
A database - Excel cannot handle concurrent editing or that volume well
Excel with the file on a shared drive
questions.explanation: Fitting is not the same as working. The volume alone would make Excel slow, but concurrent editing is the real blocker - Excel locks the file for one editor at a time. Knowing where Excel stops is part of using it well.

questions.question: What does Protected View mean when a downloaded workbook opens in it?
options: Excel has opened it in a sandbox because it came from outside your machine
questions.explanation: Protected View is a safety sandbox for files from email, the internet or another machine - formulas do not calculate and macros do not run until you choose Enable Editing. It is also why automation scripts fail on freshly downloaded files.

questions.question: You use Paste Values twenty times a day and it takes four clicks each time. What is the right fix?
options: Add Paste Values to the Quick Access Toolbar
questions.explanation: The Quick Access Toolbar gives any command a permanent one-click home, and its first ten items get Alt+1 to Alt+0 as shortcuts automatically. Twenty times a day times three saved clicks is real time.

questions.question: What does the range reference `B3:F20` describe?
options: Every cell in the rectangle from B3 to F20
questions.explanation: A colon means 'through', and the result is the whole rectangular block - here 5 columns by 18 rows, 90 cells. Reading ranges fluently is what lets you check a SUM's range at a glance instead of trusting it.

questions.question: The Formula Bar can be expanded to show a long formula over several lines.
questions.explanation: Click the small chevron at its right edge, or press Ctrl+Shift+U. Long nested formulas become readable instead of scrolling sideways, and you can press Alt+Enter inside a formula to break it onto lines deliberately.

questions.question: What does pressing Ctrl+Home do?
options: Goes to the start of the current row
questions.explanation: Ctrl+Home returns to A1 from anywhere, which is the companion to Ctrl+End. Leaving a file saved at A1 on every sheet is a small courtesy to whoever opens it next.
